figureFinding: Posterior subcapsular cataract: a granular, plaque-like opacity lying directly beneath the posterior lens capsule, best appreciated on retroillumination. It causes glare and halos around point light sources, worse vision in bright light (pupil constricted over the opacity), and near vision worse than distance.

review.explanation: A posterior subcapsular opacity sits immediately in front of the nodal point at the centre of the visual axis, so anything that constricts the pupil, bright ambient light, accommodation at near, or a miotic drop, makes the opacity occupy proportionally more of the aperture. The result is disproportionate glare and reduced vision in bright conditions and near vision that is worse than distance, which is why these patients often see better in dim light. Nuclear sclerosis instead produces gradual distance blur with a myopic shift, and cortical spokes classically cause glare from a focal light source at night.
review.concern: Options A and C are two phrasings of the same phenomenon in this recall, so the item is internally ambiguous. The defensible teaching point is bright-light and miosis-related glare; if option A was intended as glare from a focal light at night, that finding leans more towards cortical than posterior subcapsular cataract.

question: A case of a 32 years old male patient who had RD repaired by PPV and silicone oil tamponade years ago. Later, he underwent cataract removal with silicone oil removal. Afterwards, he developed high IOP unresponsive to treatments. The surgeon planned for a tube drainage implant. What is the most common complication?

options.B: High IOP due to tube blockage

explanation: The source is undecided between A and B.

review.explanation: Early hypotony with a shallow chamber and choroidal effusion is the commonest complication after glaucoma drainage device implantation, and the risk is amplified in a vitrectomised eye where there is no vitreous to resist rapid volume loss and no normal ciliary body reserve after long-standing oil tamponade. Tube occlusion is a real hazard in a silicone-oil eye and is the reason the tube is placed inferiorly when oil remains, but the oil has been removed here. Malignant glaucoma is essentially not a concern in an eye that is both aphakic or pseudophakic and vitrectomised, and suprachoroidal haemorrhage, though the most feared complication, is far less frequent than hypotony.

question: Which of the following statements regarding fornix-based versus limbal-based trabeculectomies is true?

options.A: the limbal-based approach is associated with a higher rate of wound leaks compared to the fornix-based approach
options.B: the fornix-based approach is technically more difficult compared to the limbal-based approach
options.C: the limbal-based approach has a greater chance of producing a diffuse low bleb compared to a fornix-based approach
options.D: the fornix-based approach promotes filtration of fluid more posteriorly compared to the limbal-based approach

explanation: In fornix-based trabeculectomies, the initial conjunctival incision is actually made at the limbus (yes, this terminology typically confuses new residents being first exposed to filtering surgery). Due to better exposure at the limbus, the fornix-based approach is technically easier and can be done easily without an assistant. In contrast, for limbal-based filters, the conjunctival incision is made 8-10 mm posterior to the limbus (i.e. in the fornix) which is technically more difficult due to poorer exposure. There is a greater incidence of wound leaks in fornix-based filters since the edge of the wound is at the limbus. However, fornix-based filters are thought to produce lower, more diffuse blebs since the subconjunctival scar (created by the suture line) is anterior to the scleral flap. This promotes fluid flow posterior to the flap resulting in a lower, more diffuse filtering bleb. In contrast, the scar in limbal-based filters is posterior to the scleral flap -- therefore, these blebs are typically more focal and elevated. The advantage of limbal-based filters is that wound closure is less prone to leaks since the suture line is far from the limbus. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: The naming refers to where the base of the conjunctival flap lies, not where the incision is made, which is the usual source of confusion. In a fornix-based flap the incision is at the limbus, so the eventual suture line and its scar sit anterior to the scleral flap and aqueous is directed posteriorly, producing a lower, more diffuse bleb rather than a focal cystic one. That also explains why fornix-based flaps are technically easier, with far better exposure, and why they carry the greater risk of early wound leak, since the wound edge lies at the limbus. Options A, B and C each reverse one of those relationships.

question: Post Phaco + ECP with high IOP and shallow AC and patent PI. Which of the following is improbable to help in the diagnosis:
explanation: (There was no mention of fundus examination or red reflex)

review.explanation: A shallow chamber with high pressure after phaco combined with endocyclophotocoagulation, in the presence of a patent iridotomy, is the setting for aqueous misdirection, and the workup is aimed at separating that from suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion and from ciliary body rotation. B-scan and ultrasound biomicroscopy do exactly that, imaging the suprachoroidal space and the ciliary body-lens relationship. Setting out to exclude iris bombe adds nothing once the iridotomy has been confirmed patent, because a patent iridotomy has already excluded pupillary block by definition.
review.concern: The item is ambiguous as recalled. Option D, antiglaucoma medication, is a treatment rather than a diagnostic test and could equally be argued as the thing that does not help in diagnosis. The source key is defensible only because the stem explicitly states the iridotomy is patent.

question: A diabetic with high IOP, fainted after Diamox, what could be the cause?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, producing bicarbonaturia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, so the blood pH falls. Systemic symptoms of malaise, paraesthesiae, fatigue and near-syncope follow from that acidosis, and a diabetic patient with reduced buffering reserve or impaired renal function tolerates it particularly poorly, which is why it must be used cautiously and avoided in significant renal impairment. Bicarbonate loss into the urine is a true pharmacological effect but it is the mechanism, not the reason the patient fainted, and acetazolamide does not raise blood glucose.

question: Patient with ocular melanoma post radiation treatment. VA 20/100, had high IOP despite being on full antiglaucoma medication. What to do?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Elevated pressure after plaque brachytherapy for uveal melanoma is usually neovascular or a consequence of radiation-induced anterior segment change, and the governing principle is that any procedure creating a transscleral fistula risks extraocular seeding of viable tumour cells. Trabeculectomy and tube shunts are therefore avoided in an eye that still harbours melanoma. Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation reduces aqueous production without creating an outflow tract to the subconjunctival space and is the accepted approach, ideally alongside anti-VEGF and panretinal treatment for the neovascular component. Continuing to observe on maximal medical therapy that has already failed leaves the eye at pressures that will destroy remaining vision.

question: Patient with angle closure glaucoma, you did PI, still high IOP, patient has mild cataract, what is the next step?

options.A: Do phaco because it is phacomorphic
options.B: make sure of the patency of the PI and augment if needed

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: When pressure stays high after laser iridotomy, the first duty is to confirm that the iridotomy is genuinely full thickness, ideally by seeing the anterior capsule through it or by transillumination, and to enlarge or add to it if not, then repeat gonioscopy to look for a residual non-pupillary-block mechanism such as plateau iris configuration, peripheral anterior synechiae or a lens-related component. Jumping to lens extraction on the assumption of a phacomorphic mechanism, in an eye with only mild cataract and an iridotomy of unproven patency, treats a diagnosis that has not been established. Sequence matters: confirm patency, regonio, then decide between iridoplasty, lens extraction or filtration.

question: Female, unilateral corectopia and corneal edema, what's the diagnosis?
explanation: This is the most common of the three sub-types, representing approximately 50% of all cases of ICE syndrome.[1] Of the three, Chandler Syndrome typically presents with a greater degree of corneal pathology with associated corneal edema. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: Both options are variants of the iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, which is characteristically unilateral, sporadic and commoner in middle-aged women, and in which abnormal endothelium migrates across the angle and iris. Chandler syndrome is the commonest variant and is defined by predominant endothelial decompensation, so corneal oedema and a hammered silver endothelial appearance dominate the picture, often at relatively modest pressures, with only mild corectopia. Progressive or essential iris atrophy is dominated instead by marked iris thinning, full-thickness holes, pseudopolycoria and gross corectopia, with the cornea relatively spared. The combination given here, corectopia with corneal oedema in a woman with unilateral disease, fits Chandler syndrome.

question: Hx of CRVO, presenting with HM vision, high IOP, corneal edema obscuring the view, 360 NVI and dense white cataract. What is the most appropriate definitive management (exact wording)?
explanation: The source is undecided between A and B. definitive management after clearing the view

review.explanation: This is established neovascular glaucoma after ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion, with hand movements vision, 360 degrees of iris neovascularisation and a media opacity that makes retinal laser impossible for the time being. Cyclophotocoagulation is the definitive pressure-lowering option in an eye with poor visual potential and an angle that is closed by fibrovascular membrane, and it avoids the very high failure rate of filtration in an actively neovascular eye. Panretinal photocoagulation is the correct treatment of the underlying ischaemic drive and should follow once the view allows, but it cannot be delivered through corneal oedema and a dense white cataract, and it does not by itself control an already closed angle. Topical therapy alone is not definitive, and retrobulbar alcohol is a comfort measure for a blind painful eye.
review.concern: Reasonable examiners could pick panretinal photocoagulation as the definitive treatment of the cause, which is why the source is undecided. The phrase about clearing the view first is the pivot; taken as written, cyclodestruction is the definitive procedure available now.

question: old diabetic lady, occasional unilateral blurry vision at night with halos around lights and pain. All exam normal (iop normal, no PDR findings). Gonio finding?
explanation: This patient might have had previous attacks of angle-closure.

review.explanation: Intermittent blurring with coloured haloes and ache, occurring in the evening or in dim conditions and resolving spontaneously, is the textbook history of subacute or intermittent angle closure, where mid-dilation apposes iris and trabecular meshwork and the pressure spikes transiently. Between attacks the pressure, disc and field can be entirely normal, so gonioscopy is the examination that makes the diagnosis and will show occludable, narrow angles. Peripheral anterior synechiae may accumulate after repeated attacks but are a later consequence rather than the expected finding in a normal examination, and neovascularisation of the angle would require proliferative disease, which the stem explicitly excludes.

question: A 44-year-old man presents to the emergency room with right eye decreased vision following a motor vehicle accident in which he suffered blunt trauma to his right eye. On examination his IOP is 60mmHg OD, 18mmHg OS. Fundoscopic exam is significant for a vitreous hemorrhage. Paracentesis was performed, draining 0.4 ml of fluid from the anterior chamber, which contained cellular debris and macrophages leading to eventual buildup in the trabecular network. Which of the following types of glaucoma is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation: Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: The paracentesis sample is the whole answer: macrophages laden with haemoglobin, together with cellular debris, obstructing the trabecular meshwork after intraocular haemorrhage, defines haemolytic glaucoma. Ghost cell glaucoma is a different mechanism, in which khaki-coloured, rigid, degenerated erythrocytes that have lost their intracellular haemoglobin obstruct outflow, typically weeks after a vitreous haemorrhage in a vitrectomised or post-capsulotomy eye, and the aspirate contains those cells rather than macrophages. Haemosiderotic glaucoma is a chronic process from iron toxicity to the meshwork after long-standing haemorrhage. Neovascular glaucoma requires a fibrovascular membrane in the angle, not free macrophages.

question: Best method to measure IOP in a patient who is post Lasik 6 weeks, the examination showed central opacity between the stroma and the Flap interface but you did OCT and no fluid was found in the interface?
explanation: No DCT

review.explanation: After LASIK the central cornea is thinner and biomechanically altered, and here it also carries a central interface opacity, so central applanation over that abnormal zone is the least reliable place to measure. The Tono-Pen has a small tip and can be applied to the peripheral, unablated cornea outside the flap, which is the standard workaround in post-LASIK eyes and the reason it is preferred when interface pathology is present. Goldmann and Perkins are the same applanation principle and share the same central-cornea limitations, with Perkins simply portable, and non-contact air puff tonometry is the most affected of all by altered corneal biomechanics. Dynamic contour tonometry would be ideal because it is largely thickness independent, but it is not offered.
review.concern: Note the wider teaching point the item is circling: in interface fluid syndrome, applanation reads deceptively normal or low while true pressure is very high, and peripheral measurement unmasks it. Here the OCT excludes interface fluid, so the reasoning rests on the central opacity alone.

question: Which one of the following has the highest risk of blindness in POAG?

options.C: High IOP at the time of diagnosis
options.D: Visual field loss at the time of diagnosis

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The single strongest predictor of eventual blindness in primary open-angle glaucoma is how advanced the disease already is when it is first detected, because a field that is severely damaged at presentation leaves little reserve and implies years of undetected progression. This is the rationale behind case finding and early detection programmes. Presenting pressure, thin central corneal thickness and ethnicity are all genuine risk factors for developing or progressing glaucoma, and thin corneas and African ancestry in particular carry higher risk, but none predicts blindness as powerfully as the severity of field loss already present at diagnosis. White skin colour is not a risk factor at all in this context; the higher-risk group is people of African descent.

question: One of the followings gives falsely low IOP readings:
explanation: high. Reference: AAO BCSC Glaucoma 22-23: - Corneal edema predisposes to inaccurately low readings, whereas pressure measurements taken over a corneal scar will be falsely

review.explanation: Goldmann applanation assumes a cornea of average thickness and normal rigidity, and corneal oedema makes the tissue more compliant and easier to flatten, so the instrument under-reads and true pressure is higher than the number displayed. A corneal scar behaves in the opposite way, being stiffer and harder to applanate, and gives falsely high readings, as does increased scleral or ocular rigidity. This is clinically important in an eye with corneal decompensation from a pressure spike, where a reassuring applanation figure can badly mislead.
review.concern: Options A and D are effectively the same entity in this recall, since stromal oedema is corneal oedema; the distinction the examiner intended was almost certainly oedema versus scar.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with acute severe pain in the left eye. His intraocular pressure is 50 mmHg OS and 16 mmHg OD. Slit-lamp exam OS shows a shallow anterior chamber with a subluxated lens that appears to be occluding the pupil. Which of the following procedures is most appropriate for this patient in the clinic?

options.A: 1 laser peripheral iridotomy (PI) located at 6 o'clock
options.B: 2 laser peripheral PI 90 degrees away from each other
options.D: 2 laser peripheral PI 180 degrees apart from each other

explanation: Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: A subluxated lens obstructing the pupil produces pupillary block, and the immediate in-clinic treatment is laser iridotomy to bypass it, but a mobile lens can shift with head position and occlude a single opening. Placing two iridotomies 180 degrees apart ensures that at least one remains functional whichever way the lens displaces, which is standard practice in ectopia lentis. Two iridotomies only 90 degrees apart sit within the same quadrant-to-quadrant arc and can both be covered by the same displaced lens. A single opening, whether at 6 or at 12 o clock, leaves no redundancy, and a 12 o clock iridotomy also risks symptomatic dysphotopsia if not covered by the lid.

question: Pic of ROP zone 1 with plus disease (exactly as the picture above). Based on a recent study, what is the best treatment modality?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: For zone I disease with plus disease, intravitreal bevacizumab has the better evidence base, which is what the phrase about a recent study is pointing to. The randomised trial comparing bevacizumab monotherapy with conventional laser in stage 3 plus disease found a significant reduction in recurrence for zone I eyes specifically, along with continued peripheral retinal vascularisation rather than the permanent destruction of peripheral retina and the myopic shift that ablation produces. Cryotherapy is of historical interest and was superseded by laser, and intravitreal corticosteroid has no role in ROP. The important caveat to teach alongside this is that anti-VEGF carries a real risk of late reactivation, so these infants need prolonged screening well beyond the usual endpoint, and systemic VEGF suppression remains a live concern.
review.concern: The source key of laser is standard-of-care-defensible and remains an accepted option, but it does not match the stem wording invoking a recent study, and it is the weaker choice for zone I plus disease. For posterior zone I disease specifically, anti-VEGF is now widely regarded as first line.

question: Elderly male had a sudden superior VF defect. On exam, there is a yellow plaque of inferotemporal arcade with whitening and swelling of inferior retina. What investigation would help to know the source?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A bright refractile yellow plaque at an arteriolar bifurcation with downstream retinal whitening is a Hollenhorst cholesterol embolus causing branch retinal artery occlusion, and the superior field defect matches the inferotemporal territory. The purpose of investigation is to find the embolic source, so carotid imaging for atherosclerotic plaque and cardiac assessment with ECG, looking for atrial fibrillation, plus echocardiography for valvular or mural thrombus, are what is required, alongside urgent stroke-risk assessment. Inflammatory markers are essential when giant cell arteritis is suspected, but that produces arteritic ischaemia without a visible cholesterol plaque. Brain MRI documents concurrent cerebral infarction but does not identify the embolic source.

question: A 3 yrs old child presented with respiratory distress after falling on the edge of the table according to his father. Fundus photo shows multiple retinal hemorrhages, asking what could be the cause?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Multiple retinal haemorrhages in a small child, particularly when numerous, multilayered and extending to the periphery, together with a history that does not plausibly explain the injury and with respiratory compromise suggesting an occult head injury, is abusive head trauma until proven otherwise. The mechanism is repetitive acceleration and deceleration with vitreoretinal traction, and the finding mandates urgent paediatric safeguarding referral and neuroimaging. A short fall onto a table edge does not generate that pattern. Valsalva retinopathy produces a localised premacular or sub-internal limiting membrane haemorrhage, and Purtscher retinopathy follows severe compressive chest or crush injury with cotton wool spots and Purtscher flecken rather than diffuse haemorrhages.

question: An ~ 80 yrs old man, diabetic and hypertensive, presented with decreased vision for 2 months. On exam: corneal edema, retinal arterial pulsation with retinal venous status and neovascularization of the right eye, left eye has few microaneurysms, asking what is the diagnosis (No picture)?
explanation: C

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Full description of OIS in an older vasculopathic patient: dilated retinal veins, microaneurysms, rubeosis iridis, retinal haemorrhages, and the link to severe carotid stenosis/occlusion, with workup and prognosis

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome in a patient with background Diabetic Retinopathy: Distinguishing Features - EyeRounds
referenceLinks.shows: Wide-field Optos fundus photo with corneal oedema, anterior chamber flare, narrowed arteries, mildly dilated veins and mid-peripheral dot-blot haemorrhages; explicitly discusses how asymmetry and the mid-peripheral haemorrhage distribution separate OIS from diabetic retinopathy, and lists CRVO in the differential

referenceLinks.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome - EyeRounds case 327
referenceLinks.shows: Six figures including bilateral wide-field fundus montages, OCT and cerebral angiogram; documents disc and arcade neovascularisation and a central retinal artery that occludes with very light digital pressure, with 99.5% and 100% internal carotid occlusion

figureFinding: Ocular ischemic syndrome from severe ipsilateral carotid occlusive disease: corneal oedema, anterior chamber flare, rubeosis/neovascularisation, narrowed retinal arteries with spontaneous arterial pulsation (or an artery easily occluded by light digital pressure), dilated but NON-tortuous veins, and scattered mid-peripheral dot-blot haemorrhages - all markedly asymmetric versus the fellow eye, which shows only a few microaneurysms.

review.explanation: Spontaneous retinal arterial pulsation is the discriminating sign here: it indicates that ocular perfusion pressure has fallen close to intraocular pressure, which is the hallmark of carotid occlusive disease and ocular ischaemic syndrome. Add markedly asymmetric disease with anterior segment involvement and corneal oedema in an elderly vasculopath whose fellow eye shows only trivial retinopathy, and the diagnosis follows. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is essentially symmetrical and would not explain a fellow eye with only a few microaneurysms, and central retinal vein occlusion produces widespread haemorrhages in all four quadrants with a dilated tortuous venous tree rather than arterial pulsation. Recognising ocular ischaemic syndrome matters because it carries a high mortality and requires urgent carotid and cardiovascular assessment.

question: A 32-year-old Nigerian presents with bilateral blurred vision. On examination, there are confluent yellow-white areas with associated flame-shaped hemorrhages in both eyes and perivascular sheathing and her CD4 count is 42 (normal 500-1500 cells/ul) (see image). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: A CD4 count of 42 with confluent yellow-white retinitis, haemorrhage and perivascular sheathing is cytomegalovirus retinitis, and systemic induction therapy with intravenous ganciclovir, or oral valganciclovir, is the appropriate initial treatment, alongside urgent antiretroviral therapy. Systemic treatment also protects the fellow eye and treats extraocular CMV disease, which is why it is preferred to intravitreal therapy alone at presentation. Acyclovir has no useful activity against CMV. Corticosteroid alone in an untreated profoundly immunosuppressed patient would accelerate the retinitis, and panretinal photocoagulation has no role in the acute management, being at most an adjunct for later detachment prophylaxis.

question: A patient with decrease of vision and diplopia and a fundus exam showed hyperemic and occlusive vasculitis and FFA confirming hot disc and leakage from vasculitis, what will you find also? (same exact picture)
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Occlusive retinal vasculitis with a hyperaemic, leaking disc on angiography is characteristic of Behcet disease, which typically produces recurrent explosive panuveitis with retinal vascular occlusion affecting both arteries and veins. The accompanying diplopia points to neurological involvement, and neuro-Behcet with central nervous system vasculitis, brainstem lesions and cranial nerve palsies is the systemic association to look for. Pericarditis and nephritis suggest systemic lupus erythematosus or an ANCA-associated vasculitis, both of which can cause retinal vascular disease but do not usually give this combination of occlusive vasculitis with a hot disc.

question: 3yr old boy Patient referred from peadiatric after he was diagnosed with Usher syndrome based on hearing loss and vestibular finding. On examination you found XT 35 PD. what is the most appropriate next diagnostics step?
explanation: Genetic Testing: Definitive diagnosis of Usher Syndrome type 1 involves identifying a homozygous proband mutation in the setting of positive symptoms and family history. The first gene to identify using single-gene sequencing is MYO7A. - Eyewiki

review.explanation: In a three-year-old, the retinal degeneration of Usher syndrome is often not yet visible and the child cannot cooperate with formal fields, so molecular confirmation is the practical next step, with MYO7A the first gene to interrogate in type 1 disease where profound congenital deafness and vestibular areflexia are present. Establishing the genotype guides prognosis, counselling of the family and eligibility for trials, and it also explains the exotropia, which in these children is commonly sensory. Double Maddox rod testing measures subjective torsion and is not feasible or informative at this age, and neuroimaging would only be indicated if the picture suggested a structural intracranial cause, which deafness with vestibular dysfunction and a syndromic diagnosis does not.

question: Fundus image of 2 choroidal lesions, which of the following will help you reach your diagnosis? (most likely melanoma)?
explanation: Similar to this picture - in section of choroidal melanoma and metastasis they mentioned Ultrasound is the primary diagnostic test that confirms the diagnosis of melanoma 2ac2905aa2c8e/Revi ew-of-Choroidal-Osteomas.pdf?origin=publication_detail Reference: #eyewiki + article + OQ https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ahmad- Mansour9/publication/264642482_Review_of_Choroidal_Osteomas/links/550dbe150cf

review.explanation: Standardised A-scan echography is the primary test for a suspected choroidal melanoma because it characterises internal reflectivity, and the classic melanoma pattern is a high initial spike with low to medium internal reflectivity and a steadily decreasing spike height, which is distinct from the high internal reflectivity of a haemangioma, metastasis or osteoma. B-scan adds shape information such as the collar-stud configuration and choroidal excavation, and the pair together, with measured thickness for growth surveillance, is how the diagnosis is made clinically without biopsy. OCT is excellent for subretinal fluid and overlying retinal changes but cannot see through the full thickness of a pigmented mass, and fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography give supportive but non-specific patterns.

question: IV drug abuser with perforating eye injury and signs of Endo, what's the organism?
explanation: Bacillus species are mostly seen in IV drugs users Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Endophthalmitis#Endogenous_Bacterial_Endophthalmitis

review.explanation: Bacillus cereus is the organism to fear in an intravenous drug user and in penetrating injury with soil or organic contamination, and it produces a fulminant endophthalmitis with rapid onset over hours, severe pain, ring corneal infiltrate, marked chemosis, hypopyon and often fever and leucocytosis. Because the exotoxins are destructive and the course is measured in hours, immediate vitreous sampling with intravitreal antibiotics, including vancomycin to which it is usually susceptible, and often early vitrectomy, are needed. Klebsiella is the classic organism of endogenous endophthalmitis in diabetics with pyogenic liver abscess, particularly in East Asia, rather than in this penetrating-injury and injection-drug setting.

question: Which of the following hypertensive retinal lesions are indicative of an Highest ischemic retinopathy?

options.B: venous beading and new retinal vessels
options.D: hard exudates and new retinal vessels

explanation: Chronic hypertensive retinal lesions include microaneurysms, IRMAs (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, venous venous beading, and new retinal vessels. The last two findings are signs of ischemic retinopathy.

review.explanation: Within the spectrum of chronic hypertensive retinal change, venous beading and frank retinal neovascularisation are the findings that indicate significant capillary non-perfusion, exactly as they do in diabetic retinopathy, where venous beading is one of the strongest predictors of progression to proliferative disease. Microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages and hard exudates reflect vascular leakage and chronic damage but not necessarily severe ischaemia. Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities do signal ischaemia, but each option pairing them here also contains a non-ischaemic marker, so the pairing of venous beading with new vessels is the one in which both elements indicate ischaemia.

question: Most important risk factor for the development and progression of diabetic retinopathy?
explanation: Important long-term data on disease rates and progression, including a direct association between longer duration of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and increased prevalence of diabetic retinopathy, were provided by the WESDR (Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy) Among WESDR participants with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus, nearly 99% of those with type 1 disease and 60% of those with type 2 disease had some degree of diabetic retinopathy. PDR was also reported in 50% of patients with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes and in 25% of those with a 25- year history of type 2 diabetes. In addition, a visual acuity of 20/200 or worse was observed in 3.6% of patients with younger-onset disease (ie, aged <30 years at diagnosis) and 1.6% of patients with older-onset disease (ie, aged 30 years or older at diagnosis). This vision loss was attributed to diabetic retinopathy in 86% of the younger- onset group and 33% of the older-onset group. AAO retina

review.explanation: Duration of diabetes is the single strongest predictor of both the presence and the severity of diabetic retinopathy, as shown by the Wisconsin epidemiological data in which nearly all patients with type 1 diabetes of twenty years duration had some retinopathy. That is why screening intervals are anchored to duration and to time since diagnosis. The important nuance to teach is that duration is not modifiable, whereas glycaemic control is the most important modifiable risk factor and tight control demonstrably slows onset and progression; hypertension and dyslipidaemia are additional modifiable contributors, with lipids particularly linked to hard exudate and maculopathy.

question: What type of laser is preferred in case of vitreous hemorrhage?
explanation: hemorrhages better than lasers with other wavelengths do. which makes it suitable for treatment of subretinal neovascular membrane. photocoagulation is performed, if possible through the residual hemorrhage, to cause regression of neovascularization. A krypton laser may aid photocoagulation as it passes through hemorrhage better than argon lasers. Reference: AAO: https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/vitreous-hemorrhage- diagnosistreatment-2: - If neovascularization from proliferative retinopathy is the cause, laser panretinal

review.explanation: Longer wavelengths scatter and are absorbed less by blood, so krypton red at 647 nm penetrates residual vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage far better than shorter wavelengths and still reaches the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid to produce a burn. Blue-green argon light is strongly absorbed by haemoglobin and by xanthophyll and is largely wasted in the haemorrhage, and it is avoided near the fovea for the same reason. Yellow dye laser is well absorbed by oxyhaemoglobin, which is useful for treating vessels but a disadvantage when trying to treat through blood. In modern practice the 810 nm diode is used for the same reason as krypton red.

question: A 75-year-old woman is referred to you by the emergency room for "painless loss of vision" in the left eye. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 and 20/40 in the right and left eyes respectively. There is a brisk afferent pupillary defect in the left eye. Your exam is significant for the findings seen above. A fluorescein angiogram (FA) is performed (frame at 25 seconds shown above). The blood supply preserving this woman's central acuity is a branch most directly from which artery? (same exact Pic)
explanation: The fundus photo shows retinal whitening but with preservation of perfusion in the foveal area. The corresponding FA shows absence of dye in the majority of the retinal blood vessels except for a few vessels feeding the fovea. This presentation is consistent with a cilioretinal-sparing central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The blood supply to the inner layers of the retina is typically derived entirely from the central retinal artery (CRA). The exception is that approximately 1530% of eyes have a cilioretinal artery which is a branch most directly from the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs). The CRA, PCAs, and lacrimal artery are branches of the ophthalmic artery. Most cases of CRAO are visually-devastating with greater than two-thirds of cases having visual acuity of worse than 20/400. The majority of CRAO cases associated with good central visual acuity are those with a patent cilioretinal artery. Vision of NLP typically does not occur in CRAO, but can occur with simultaneous choroidal infarction (e.g. ophthalmic artery occlusion).

review.explanation: Retinal whitening with a preserved perfused island at the fovea, and an angiogram showing delayed filling of the retinal circulation except for a vessel supplying the papillomacular region, is a central retinal artery occlusion with cilioretinal sparing. A cilioretinal artery is present in roughly a fifth to a third of eyes and arises from the posterior ciliary circulation, not from the central retinal artery, which is why it stays perfused and preserves central acuity when the central retinal artery occludes. The central retinal artery, the posterior ciliary arteries and the lacrimal artery are all branches of the ophthalmic artery, but the question asks for the vessel from which the cilioretinal branch arises most directly, which is the posterior ciliary artery.

question: Strongest HLA association?
explanation: #nature journal The association between HLA-A29 and birdshot chorioretinopathy is the strongest association between HLA and disease ever described https://www.nature.com/articles/eye1990133.pdf:

review.explanation: The link between HLA-A29 and birdshot chorioretinopathy is one of the strongest HLA-disease associations described in medicine, with well over ninety percent of patients positive and a relative risk far exceeding that of any other ocular HLA association, which is why HLA-A29 testing is effectively part of the diagnostic criteria. HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and with acute anterior uveitis, but the relative risk is an order of magnitude lower, and the majority of B27-positive individuals never develop disease. Psoriasis is more closely linked to HLA-Cw6, with B27 relevant mainly to the spondylitic and psoriatic arthritis subgroup, so that pairing is the weakest of the three.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with ocular pain and photophobia for 1 week. Her visual acuity is 20/30 OU, and IOP is 50 mm Hg OU. Slit-lamp findings are presented below. (see image). What is the most likely etiology of this patient's condition?
explanation: Note on the source's marking: DISPUTED MARKING: a handwritten Arabic annotation in blue ink sits beside the options reading 'ع الغالب هذي غلط، !؟' (roughly 'this is probably wrong, ?!'), i.e. the annotator questions the checkmarked answer. The checkmark on 'Herpes uveitis' is the only answer marker present. Includes a two-panel slit-lamp image (diffuse and slit view) with arrows pointing to pigmented keratic precipitates. Options carry no letters in the source; letters A-D assigned by display order. Source spelling 'Fuch's heteromatic iridocyclitis' kept verbatim. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Anterior uveitis with pain, photophobia and markedly raised intraocular pressure in the presence of active inflammation is the signature of herpetic trabeculitis, where the meshwork is inflamed rather than clogged, and pigmented or stellate keratic precipitates support it. That combination, high pressure with active anterior chamber inflammation, is unusual in most other uveitides, where the pressure is typically normal or low from ciliary hyposecretion. HLA-B27 uveitis characteristically produces a fibrinous non-granulomatous reaction with hypotony rather than pressures of 50, sarcoidosis gives mutton-fat precipitates with normal or low pressure in most cases, and Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis has small stellate precipitates scattered over the whole endothelium but is white, painless and photophobia free, with glaucoma developing chronically rather than acutely.
review.concern: The recalled stem states the pressure is 50 in both eyes, which is atypical for herpetic disease, classically unilateral. Bilateral hypertensive anterior uveitis with pigmented precipitates would raise CMV anterior uveitis, still a herpesvirus, so option C remains the best of those offered, but the handwritten doubt beside the key in the source is understandable.

question: A scenario about pars planitis asking about the content of snow banking?
explanation: Histologic studies show condensed vitreous, fibroblasts, lymphocytes, and lymphocyte cuffing of the peripheral retinal veins. Snowbanks and snowballs consist of a fibrovascular layer containing mononuclear leukocytes and fibrocyte-like cells, as well as vitreous collagen, Muller cells and fibrous astrocytes. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Intermediate_Uveitis

review.explanation: The snowbank of pars planitis is an organised fibrovascular and fibroglial membrane over the pars plana and peripheral retina, made up of condensed vitreous collagen, fibroblasts and fibrous astrocytes, Muller cell processes and new vessels, with only scattered mononuclear leucocytes. Its vascular content is why snowbanks can bleed and why vitreous haemorrhage and tractional complications occur, and it is why cryotherapy or peripheral laser can be used for refractory neovascular snowbanks. Multinucleated giant cells belong to granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis rather than to the snowbank itself, and cystoid macular oedema is the commonest cause of visual loss in pars planitis but is a separate complication, not the content of the snowbank.

question: A 32-year-old woman reports one week of floaters in her left eye. She denies flashes of light or sudden trauma. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices a mild anterior chamber reaction and peripheral snowballs and snowbanks in the affected eye. What tests would be most appropriate to order?

options.A: HLA-B27, RPR, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.B: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), Toxoplasma IgG and IgM, and Lyme titers
options.C: Toxoplasma IgG and IgM, serum angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE), and rapid plasma reagin (RPR)

explanation: The findings noted suggest pars planitis. The differential diagnosis for this includes sarcoidosis, syphilis, toxocariasis, lyme disease, multiple sclerosis, and tuberculosis. Toxoplasmosis does not cause pars planitis, nor does HLA-B27-associated uveitis. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Snowballs and snowbanking in a young adult define intermediate uveitis, and the differential that changes management is multiple sclerosis, syphilis, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis and tuberculosis. MRI of the brain looks for demyelinating lesions, since a proportion of these patients have or will develop multiple sclerosis and that alters both prognosis and the choice of systemic agent, while RPR excludes syphilis and Lyme serology is appropriate in endemic areas. Toxoplasmosis produces a focal necrotising retinochoroiditis adjacent to an old scar with overlying vitritis, not snowbanking, so any option containing toxoplasma serology is a distractor, and HLA-B27 relates to acute anterior uveitis rather than intermediate disease. Serum ACE for sarcoidosis would be a defensible addition, but it appears only paired with toxoplasma testing.

question: Child Lt Hypertropia with right head tilt for a long time. No Excyclotorsion. What is the management:

options.A: Left IO weakinning Right SR recession

explanation: Similar question but not exactly the same:

referenceLinks.title: Three Step Test for Cyclovertical Muscle Palsy - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Figure 1 is a clinical photograph of a superior oblique palsy in the nine diagnostic gaze positions; Figure 2 is an annotated three-step-test diagram; Figure 3 shows double Maddox rod testing for torsion. Explains why head tilt to the palsied side worsens the hypertropia

referenceLinks.title: Cranial Nerve 4 Palsy - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical description of ipsilateral hypertropia with excyclotorsion and a compensatory head tilt away from the affected muscle, the Parks-Bielschowsky-Helveston three-step test, congenital versus acquired aetiology, and management options

figureFinding: Long-standing (congenital) LEFT superior oblique / fourth nerve palsy: left hypertropia that increases in right gaze and on LEFT head tilt, with a compensatory head tilt to the RIGHT (away from the palsied side). Subjective excyclotorsion is typically absent in congenital cases because of long-standing sensory adaptation. The photo should show a child with a habitual head tilt and a higher left eye.

review.explanation: A long-standing left hypertropia with a compensatory head tilt to the right is the classic posture of a left superior oblique palsy, and the absence of subjective excyclotorsion despite objective torsion is itself evidence of chronicity, since congenital cases develop large sensory and fusional adaptations. When the deviation is modest and there is overaction of the ipsilateral inferior oblique, weakening that inferior oblique, the direct antagonist on the affected side, is the standard first operation. A resection of the right inferior rectus would further depress the lower of the two eyes and increase the left hypertropia, so it is the wrong direction of correction.
review.concern: The option set is corrupted: option B is missing entirely and option A appears to fuse two separate procedures, left inferior oblique weakening and right superior rectus recession, the second of which would worsen rather than correct a left hypertropia. Only the inferior oblique weakening component is defensible.

question: African boy, with light skin and blond hair and gray eyes, mother and father normal but the father's brother has similar condition, mother is pregnant and asking what's the risk for her next child?
explanation: Oculocutaneous albinism is inherited in the AR pattern

review.explanation: Generalised hypopigmentation of skin, hair and eyes in a child of African parentage with two unaffected parents and an affected paternal uncle is oculocutaneous albinism inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Because the couple already has an affected child, both parents are obligate heterozygous carriers, so each subsequent pregnancy carries a one in four, or 25 percent, recurrence risk regardless of the sex of the child. A figure under one percent would apply to a sporadic or new dominant mutation, 50 percent to autosomal dominant inheritance from an affected parent, and 75 percent corresponds to the chance of being unaffected in this pedigree rather than affected.

question: Jerk Nystagmus OS with large left head turn, Frensel prism glasses options to reduce the head turn:

options.A: Base In OD, Base in OS
options.B: Base out OD, base out OS
options.C: Base In OD, Base out OS
options.D: Base out OD, base in OS

explanation: You want to turn the prisms toward the null point (right gaze)

review.explanation: A large left face turn means the child is holding the eyes in right gaze to reach the null zone, where the nystagmus damps and acuity is best. To let the head come straight, prisms must make a straight-ahead target appear as if it lies to the right, so that the eyes rotate into right gaze to fixate it. A prism displaces the image towards its apex, so the apex must point right and the bases must point left, which for the right eye is base in and for the left eye is base out. The practical rule that follows is that the bases are oriented in the direction of the face turn and the apices towards the null point, and both eyes must be prismed in the same direction in space so that binocular alignment is not disturbed.

question: You are called to see a 3-day-old child for possible neonatal conjunctivitis of both eyes. During the course of your complete eye exam, you detect a mild amount of intraretinal hemorrhages OU on dilated fundus exam. The child otherwise appears healthy and attentive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this child?

options.B: hematologic workup for possible coagulation disorder
options.C: imaging for other evidence of non-accidental trauma
options.D: report this incident immediately to child protective services

explanation: Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Retinal haemorrhages are found in a substantial minority of healthy newborns after vaginal delivery, are usually intraretinal, mild and bilateral, and resolve spontaneously within days to a few weeks without sequelae. In an otherwise well, alert three-day-old with no other injury, this is a birth-related finding and observation with documentation is correct. Escalating to a coagulation screen, skeletal survey or a child protection referral at three days of age on the basis of mild birth haemorrhages alone is disproportionate. The situation is entirely different beyond the neonatal period or when the haemorrhages are numerous, multilayered, extending to the periphery or accompanied by retinoschisis or encephalopathy, when abusive head trauma must be excluded urgently.

question: Patient is Ortho at distance and exophoria at near, +0.25 refraction, what not to give?

options.D: give plus lens more than his refraction

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Orthophoria at distance with exophoria at near and an essentially plano refraction is convergence insufficiency, and every effective treatment works by increasing convergence, either by training fusional convergence or by forcing it. Pencil push-ups and stereogram or vergence exercises train fusional convergence directly, and base-out prism used as therapy stimulates convergence by displacing the image outwards. Adding plus power beyond the refractive need does the opposite: it relaxes accommodation, and through the accommodative convergence to accommodation relationship reduces accommodative convergence, worsening the near exodeviation. Plus at near is the correct tool for the mirror problem, high AC over A convergence excess esotropia, not for convergence insufficiency.

question: Which one can be used to assess vision in preverbal child?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Teller acuity cards use forced-choice preferential looking, exploiting an infant's innate preference for a patterned over a uniform field, so they require no verbal response and can be used from early infancy. Snellen letters require literacy, and both Allen pictures and the HOTV matching test require a verbal or matching response and cooperation typically from around two and a half to three years, so none is suitable in a preverbal child. It is worth remembering that preferential looking tends to overestimate acuity in amblyopia relative to recognition acuity, so it complements rather than replaces later optotype testing.

question: a 21-year-old college student presents to your office for new-onset esotropia and diplopia symptoms. She states that this is finals week and needs to get her "eyes fixed" for her examinations. VA is 20/100 at distance and J1+ at near OU. She measures 15 PD of ET at both distance and near. Her ductions are full OU on monocular testing but she has abduction deficit OU on versions. Her pupils measure 2 mm and do not constrict well to light. Her manifest refraction is -3.00 Sphere OU, but she refuses dilation or cycloplegia due to her need to study and take her exams. Which of the following most likely describes her condition?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The triad that settles this is esotropia with pseudo-abduction deficit, miosis and pseudomyopia in a stressed young adult. Ductions being full when each eye is tested alone, while abduction appears limited on versions, is the hallmark that distinguishes spasm of the near reflex from a true sixth nerve palsy, and the miotic poorly reactive pupils and the manifest myopia that would vanish under cycloplegia complete the picture of sustained triad activation. Accommodative insufficiency causes near blur without esotropia or miosis, Horner syndrome gives unilateral miosis with ptosis and no motility deficit, and divergence insufficiency produces a comitant esotropia greater at distance with normal pupils and normal versions. Cycloplegic refraction is both diagnostic and the first step in management, which is why her refusal is deliberately placed in the stem.

question: Scenario about Marcus-Gunn jaw winking Which of the following nerve involvement in aberrant regeneration of third nerve:
explanation: trigeminal nerve supply the lateral pterygoid by mandibular nerve (CCDD), is a synkinetic syndrome in which the eyelid elevates with movement of the jaw (Video 16-1); it may present with ptosis. The synkinesis is thought to be caused by aberrant connections between the motor division of cranial nerve (CN) V and the levator muscle. Reference: AAO BCSC Pediatrics 22-23: - Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome, a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder

review.explanation: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which fibres of the motor division of the trigeminal nerve, supplying the pterygoid muscles, are misdirected to the levator palpebrae superioris, so that jaw movement, chewing or sucking elevates the ptotic lid. The nerve involved is therefore cranial nerve five. Cranial nerve seven mediates a different synkinesis, seen in aberrant regeneration after facial palsy and in the crocodile tears phenomenon, and cranial nerve eight has no motor supply to the lid or jaw.
review.concern: The stem calls this aberrant regeneration of the third nerve, which is inaccurate: jaw-winking is a congenital miswiring between the trigeminal motor branch and the levator, not acquired third nerve aberrant regeneration. The intended answer is unaffected.

question: Motorcycle trauma, pt had diplopia, right hypertropia that is more prominent on down gaze, restriction of in right gaze dextro-depression, what muscle is most likely entrapped?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The key to entrapment questions is that a muscle tethered in a fracture acts as a leash, restricting movement away from its own field of action rather than towards it. Here the right eye is hypertropic and the deviation worsens on downgaze with limitation of depression, which means the eye cannot be pulled down, so the tethered muscle is an elevator, the right superior rectus, as occurs with an orbital roof fracture in high-energy trauma such as a motorcycle collision. The much commoner orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment produces exactly the opposite pattern, a hypotropia of the affected eye with limited elevation that worsens in upgaze, together with the oculocardiac reflex in white-eyed blowouts. Forced duction testing confirms the restriction and distinguishes it from a paretic cause.
review.concern: The stem wording is garbled and the third option is truncated, so the intended muscle list cannot be fully verified, but the mechanics of a hypertropia worse in downgaze with restricted depression admit only a tethered elevator.

question: 23yr old presented with CN 4 palsy, presence of which of the following will r/o congenital CN IV palsy?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Congenital fourth nerve palsy is characterised by longstanding adaptation, and the single most useful positive marker is a large vertical fusional amplitude, often ten prism dioptres or more against a normal value of only two or three, because the visual system has had years to expand it. A low vertical fusional amplitude therefore argues strongly against a congenital cause and points to a recently acquired palsy. Facial asymmetry and a head tilt visible in old photographs are supportive evidence for a congenital palsy rather than against it, and the absence of a trauma history is unhelpful, since many acquired fourth nerve palsies follow minor or forgotten head injury or are microvascular.

question: Movement of eye in which of the following optokinetic drum direction will confirm the diagnosis of "convergence retraction Nystagmus" (Dorsal midbrain syndrome)?
explanation: Oculoplasty:

review.explanation: Convergence-retraction nystagmus in dorsal midbrain syndrome is elicited by attempted upward saccades, so the manoeuvre is to provoke repeated upward refixation. Rotating the optokinetic drum so that the stripes travel downwards drives a downward slow pursuit phase followed by an upward corrective fast phase, and it is those repeated upward saccades that bring out the co-contraction of the horizontal recti with convergence and globe retraction. Rotating the stripes upwards would generate downward fast phases and would not provoke the sign, and moving the drum towards or away from the patient tests convergence and accommodation rather than vertical saccades.

question: Female with ptosis and difficulty swallowing, what's the inheritance pattern?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Progressive ptosis with dysphagia, usually beginning in the fifth or sixth decade, is oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, which is autosomal dominant and caused by a short trinucleotide repeat expansion in the PABPN1 gene, with a founder effect in French-Canadian and certain other populations. The practical teaching point is that the dysphagia is the dangerous element, with aspiration risk, and that ptosis surgery must be conservative because of the coexisting weak orbicularis and poor Bell phenomenon. Mitochondrial inheritance would fit chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia or Kearns-Sayre syndrome, in which ophthalmoplegia rather than dysphagia dominates, and neither X-linked nor sporadic inheritance characterises this condition.

question: Case of a patient having symptoms of severe eye irritation. On examination found to have rubbing lashes of the lower lid with positive snapback test. What is the mechanism that has a play in this scenario?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A positive snapback test, in which the lower lid fails to return promptly against the globe after being pulled away without a blink, is the specific bedside sign of horizontal eyelid laxity from stretched canthal tendons and tarsus, and that laxity is the dominant mechanism allowing the lid margin and lashes to turn inward. Involutional entropion is multifactorial: horizontal laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis over the pretarsal portion. Option B fuses those last two mechanisms into a phrase that does not exist, since it is the orbicularis that overrides and the retractors that dehisce. A weak preseptal orbicularis (C) contributes to lid eversion problems rather than entropion, and levator dehiscence (D) causes aponeurotic ptosis of the upper lid, and neither is what the snapback test measures.

question: Female patient present with swelling at the lacrimal sac given oral abx came 3 days later with worsening of the symptoms (extended to adjacent structures and fluctuating mass), asking what to do next?

options.C: Irrigation of canalicular and lacrimal system

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Deterioration after three days of oral antibiotics, with spread beyond the sac into adjacent tissues, means oral therapy has failed and the acute dacryocystitis has become a periorbital or preseptal cellulitis, so the patient should be admitted for intravenous antibiotics with imaging if orbital extension is suspected. Probing or irrigating the lacrimal system (C) is contraindicated in acute infection because it risks disseminating the infection and creating a false passage. DCR (D) is the definitive treatment for the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction but is deferred until the acute inflammation has settled. Incision and drainage (A) is not wrong in principle and is appropriate for a pointing, fluctuant lacrimal sac abscess, but it is an adjunct performed under systemic antibiotic cover rather than the single next step; in practice most patients are admitted, started on intravenous antibiotics, and drained during the same admission.

question: Regarding lacrimal gland biopsy, which one is true?

options.A: It lies on fossa in lacrimal bone
options.B: Orbital part can be seen with eyelid eversion
options.C: Both orbital and palpebral ducts pass through the palpebral lobe

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The ductules draining the orbital lobe pass through or alongside the palpebral lobe before opening into the superior fornix, so secretion from the entire gland funnels through the palpebral lobe region. That single anatomical fact is exactly why a biopsy should be taken from the orbital lobe rather than the palpebral lobe, making D false: cutting the palpebral lobe can transect the ductules of the whole gland and produce a dry eye. The lacrimal gland sits in the lacrimal gland fossa of the frontal bone (A is false), whereas the lacrimal sac fossa is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla. Eyelid eversion exposes the palpebral lobe, not the orbital lobe, so B is also false.

question: Exactly this picture and asking what surgery would you do after removal?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: I cannot see the lesion, so this is answered on principle. Reconstruction of a full-thickness eyelid defect is chosen by defect size relative to total lid length: up to roughly a quarter to a third can usually be closed directly, and more in an elderly patient with lax lids; about a third to a half needs the closure relaxed with lateral cantholysis or a Tenzel semicircular flap; and beyond half a lid-sharing procedure such as a Hughes or Cutler-Beard flap with a graft is required. If the photograph shows a small, well-defined lid margin tumour, primary closure is the expected answer, and it is always the preferred option when the wound can be apposed without tension or lid margin notching.
review.concern: The answer depends on a lesion photograph I cannot see. If the tumour occupies more than about a third of the lid margin, the semicircular Tenzel flap becomes the correct choice.

question: Large salmon patch of the conjunctiva (clinical and histopathology pictures). No mention of systemic involvement. No mention of laterality. What is the treatment? (same picture exaclty)
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

referenceLinks.title: Conjunctival Lymphoma - EyeRounds case 243
referenceLinks.shows: Four clinical figures - external photos of the raised pink caruncular lesion with ptosis, a slit-lamp photo of the salmon-coloured patch with telangiectatic vessels, the classic salmon-pink appearance, and post-treatment photos. Documents treatment with external beam radiotherapy (24 Gy in 15 fractions) with excellent response; biopsy confirmed extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

referenceLinks.title: Atlas Entry - Conjunctival lymphoma - EyeRounds
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photograph of the smooth, mobile, salmon-coloured fleshy mass; biopsy-confirmed MALT lymphoma, with a companion link to benign conjunctival lymphoid hyperplasia for comparison

referenceLinks.title: Conjunctival Lymphoma - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Text reference confirming the salmon-coloured mass, the histopathology/flow cytometry workup, and that external beam radiotherapy (20-50 Gy) is the treatment of choice for indolent EMZL/FL - which is why the answer is radiotherapy, not observation or excision

figureFinding: Conjunctival lymphoma: a smooth, mobile, salmon-pink fleshy subconjunctival patch/mass (typically fornix or bulbar conjunctiva, often with telangiectatic surface vessels), plus histopathology showing a dense monotonous infiltrate of small lymphocytes - most often extranodal marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphoma. Treated with external beam radiotherapy for localised indolent disease.

review.explanation: A large salmon-pink conjunctival patch with a dense monotonous lymphoid infiltrate on histology is conjunctival lymphoma, usually of extranodal marginal zone (MALT) type. Once systemic imaging and haematological staging have excluded disseminated disease, localized low-dose external beam radiotherapy is the standard treatment for a large ocular adnexal lesion and achieves high rates of local control. Observation (A) is reserved for small indolent lesions or patients unfit for treatment; excision alone (D) is diagnostic rather than curative because the infiltrate is diffuse and margins cannot be cleared; and systemic chemotherapy or rituximab (C) is directed at disseminated disease. The examinable sequence is biopsy, then systemic staging, then local radiotherapy, because finding systemic disease switches management from local to systemic therapy.

question: A case of a pregnant woman who had a lesion for a long time that increased in size during the previous months. She is presenting with proptosis and hypermetropia and CT shows enhanced retrobulbar homogeneous encapsulated lesion, what's the diagnosis? (with fundus photo and similar pathology pics to this one)
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A well-circumscribed, encapsulated, homogeneously enhancing intraconal mass causing slowly progressive axial proptosis with an acquired hyperopic shift, the latter from indentation and shortening of the posterior globe, is the classic profile of orbital cavernous haemangioma, now more properly called cavernous venous malformation. Enlargement during pregnancy is characteristic, since these lesions expand with hormonal change and increased blood volume. Lipodermoid (B) is a congenital epibulbar choristoma of the superotemporal fornix, not a retrobulbar enhancing mass. Lymphangioma (C) is irregular and non-encapsulated and usually presents in childhood with abrupt proptosis from haemorrhage into a chocolate cyst, and solitary fibrous tumour or haemangiopericytoma (D) is far rarer, grows faster and has less well-defined margins.

question: Mechanism of TAO:
explanation: the presumed mechanism is activation of orbital fibroblasts by Graves' disease-related autoantibodies, which lead to the release of T cell chemoattractants, initiating an interaction which ultimately results in fibroblasts expressing extracellular matrix molecules, biologic materials proliferating and differentiating into myofibroblasts or lipofibroblasts and deposition of glycosaminoglycans which bind water that lead to swelling, congestion in addition to connective tissue remodeling. This results in extraocular muscle enlargement and orbital fat expansion. Reference: https://eyewiki.org/Thyroid_Eye_Disease

review.explanation: Thyroid eye disease is driven by autoantigens shared between the thyroid and the orbital fibroblast, principally the TSH receptor together with the IGF-1 receptor. Autoantibody engagement of those fibroblast receptors triggers glycosaminoglycan secretion, fibroblast proliferation, and differentiation into adipocytes or myofibroblasts, and the resulting hydrophilic matrix and fat expansion enlarge the extraocular muscles and orbital fat to produce proptosis and congestion. A cell-mediated component is genuinely present, since activated fibroblasts release T cell chemoattractants and the two populations amplify each other, so option A is not biologically false, merely not the initiating event the question is after. The clinical proof of the fibroblast receptor hypothesis is the efficacy of teprotumumab, an IGF-1 receptor blocking antibody.

question: 80yr dark-skinned brought by his daughter with the complaint of a black spot in his eye that is getting darker over years. On exam, light brown perilimbal and interpalpebral bulbar conj pigmentation (no photo given), what to do?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Flat, light brown, perilimbal and interpalpebral conjunctival pigmentation in an elderly darkly pigmented patient is complexion-associated (racial) melanosis, which is benign, usually bilateral, moves freely over the sclera, and requires only observation with baseline photographs and periodic review. The features that would instead demand action are nodularity or thickening, feeder vessels, involvement of the palpebral conjunctiva, fornix or caruncle, or new pigmentation arising in a lightly pigmented adult, none of which is described. Metastatic work-up (A) and PSA (B) chase a systemic malignancy for which there is no evidence here. Wide excision with 4 mm margins (D) is the approach to conjunctival melanoma and would be substantial over-treatment; the slow darkening over years is a reason to document photographically and follow, not to excise.

question: Which can be a part of management of botox?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Botulinum toxin chemodenervation is an established temporizing treatment for spastic entropion, where injection into the pretarsal and preseptal orbicularis stops the muscle riding up and inverting the lid margin while definitive surgery is planned. It does not treat ptosis (C); it causes ptosis when it diffuses to the levator. It has no accepted role in Marcus Gunn jaw winking (B), which is a misdirected trigeminal to levator synkinesis managed surgically. Lagophthalmos (D) deserves a caveat, because toxin is deliberately used to induce a protective ptosis in paralytic lagophthalmos with exposure keratopathy, so that option is defensible too; entropion remains the best single answer because it is the classical oculoplastic toxin indication.
review.concern: Option D is also a legitimate use of botulinum toxin (induced protective ptosis in paralytic lagophthalmos), so the item as recalled has two arguably correct answers.

question: You were called to see a patient admitted for 2 days with orbital cellulitis who started to have a sudden drop in vision, what's the most important next step?

options.A: Ask about duration of visual loss

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A sudden fall in vision in a patient being treated for orbital cellulitis means an orbital or subperiosteal abscess, orbital compartment syndrome, or intracranial or cavernous sinus extension until proven otherwise, and urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain is what identifies a collection needing surgical drainage and prompts a change in antibiotic cover. Asking about the duration of visual loss (A) does not alter the immediate plan. Measuring intraocular pressure (B) is by no means wasted and should happen at the bedside in the same minute, because tense proptosis with a markedly raised pressure and an afferent pupillary defect is orbital compartment syndrome requiring immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis before any scan. As a single best answer, urgent imaging is the step that changes management for the most likely underlying cause.

question: A 71-year-old man presents with concerns about a mass which appeared about 6 months ago, and has slowly enlarged to the point that it now protrudes between his lids. As shown in the photo, exam finds a glistening yellow mass which is painless, soft, and mobile beneath the conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (Exact Picture)
explanation: This newly-developed, soft, glistening, yellow, mobile sub-conjunctival mass is prolapsed orbital fat. In contrast, lipodermoid (aka dermolipoma) (choice "A") is a congenital choristoma comprised of dense fibroconnective tissue and fat, which would have been present since birth, rather than appearing at age 71. Lipodermoids are occasionally associated with oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia (i.e. Goldenhar syndrome). Hemangiopericytoma (choice "B") would be a firm mass, usually located in the retrobulbar intraconal space. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice "D") of the orbit forms a firm mass arising from the lacrimal gland, often causing the appearance of superotemporal lid fullness or non-axial proptosis rather than a sub-conjunctival mass.

review.explanation: A soft, mobile, glistening yellow subconjunctival mass appearing in a 71-year-old and slowly prolapsing between the lids is orbital fat herniating anteriorly through an attenuated Tenon capsule, typically in the superotemporal quadrant and more common in older or heavier patients. Lipodermoid (A) is a congenital choristoma present from birth at the lateral canthal region, so it cannot appear de novo at 71. Solitary fibrous tumour or haemangiopericytoma (B) is a firm retrobulbar mass presenting with proptosis, and lacrimal gland pleomorphic adenoma (D) is a firm superotemporal orbital mass producing non-axial proptosis and lid fullness, not a soft yellow subconjunctival lesion. The management point is that prolapsed fat is benign and only needs excision for comfort or cosmesis.

question: GCA Scenario (loss of vision in an elderly patient with pain in the temporal area and was planned for biopsy). She is concerned regarding the therapy management because she is a diabetic. What is your initial management (EXACT WORDING)?

options.C: 0.5 gm methylprednisolone IV OD for 3 days
options.D: Oral prednisone 40 mg/kg slow tapering + MTX 7.5 fast tapering up

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Giant cell arteritis with established visual loss is the one presentation where pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone is preferred to starting with oral prednisone, because the fellow eye is at high risk over the following days and the aim is maximal immediate suppression; usual regimens are 0.5 to 1 g daily for three days followed by oral prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day. Oral prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily (A and B) is the correct starting therapy for giant cell arteritis without visual involvement, which is why B is the tempting answer here. Option D is internally impossible, since 40 mg/kg of prednisone is not a real dose and methotrexate is a weak steroid-sparing adjunct rather than an initial rescue drug. Treatment must never wait for the temporal artery biopsy, which stays positive for one to two weeks after steroids are begun, and in a diabetic patient the answer is to treat and cover the glycaemia, with tocilizumab considered early as the steroid-sparing agent.
review.concern: The source key of 60 mg oral prednisone is the standard regimen for giant cell arteritis without visual loss. This patient has established visual loss, and guideline practice is intravenous pulse methylprednisolone first, then oral prednisone. Diabetes is a reason to plan glycaemic cover and early steroid-sparing therapy, not to withhold pulse steroid. I flag this at moderate strength only because the recall may have intended a stem without established visual loss.

question: weeks ago lasted 1 day No diplopia No ptosis Eom full VA 20/20 Pupil reactive to light OD: 5 to 3mm OS: 6.5mm to 5.5 Direct and indirect consensual were normal

options.C: Reassurance and OPD observation D Check for organophosphate toxicity

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: A migraineur with an episodically larger pupil that still reacts to light, full ocular motility, no ptosis and 20/20 acuity fits benign episodic unilateral mydriasis, a recognized migraine-associated phenomenon of transient autonomic imbalance, and the appropriate response is reassurance with outpatient review. A compressive third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm can be set aside because it presents with ptosis and a motility deficit alongside a poorly reactive pupil, so urgent MRI and MRA (A) is not mandated by this examination. Admission (B) adds nothing when the examination is otherwise normal, and organophosphate toxicity (D) produces miosis, not mydriasis. It remains correct to ask about inadvertent contact with anticholinergic agents and to look for the light-near dissociation and sectoral palsy of a tonic pupil, and to review promptly if any new sign appears.

question: Morning glory anomaly pic (same photo) and asking what is the associated possible vision with?
explanation: Visual acuity can vary from normal 20/20 to very poor(20/200 to count fingers) depending on the extent of optic nerve anomaly. Patients often have visual field defects, commonly enlarged blind spots.

review.explanation: Vision in morning glory disc anomaly is unpredictable and spans nearly the whole range, from near-normal 20/20 down to light perception, depending on how much of the optic nerve and papillomacular bundle is involved, so the option stating the widest realistic range is correct. Most affected eyes in practice sit around 20/100 to 20/200 with an enlarged blind spot, but quoting a narrow band such as better than 20/80 (A) or hand motions to counting fingers (D) misrepresents the variability, and no light perception (B) is not the rule. The associations that matter clinically are serous retinal detachment in roughly a third of eyes, and basal encephalocele, midline central nervous system anomalies and moyamoya disease, so neuroimaging is indicated in these children.

question: A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Bilateral severe visual loss on waking from prolonged cardiac or spinal surgery, with poorly reactive pupils and a completely normal fundus, is perioperative posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, in which the infarct is retrobulbar so the discs look normal for four to six weeks before pallor develops. Prolonged operative time, hypotension, anaemia, large fluid shifts and raised venous pressure are the recognized risk factors. Both anterior forms (B and C) are excluded by the normal fundus, since anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy requires disc oedema at presentation, and simultaneous bilateral arteritic disease in this setting would be exceptional. Dorsal midbrain syndrome (D) does produce light-near dissociation, but with upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and preserved acuity rather than hand motions vision.

explanation: The source is undecided between C and B. junctional scotoma Anterior to chiasm The pic was similar to this but but instead of 24-2 it was 30-2:

This maps directly onto all four answer options
